summary: The respondent strongly exhibits reflexivity and responsiveness, particularly in the later part of the interview where they candidly evaluate their own past complacency regarding procurement processes. Responsiveness is demonstrated through both a negative framing of rigid, fear-driven evaluation criteria and a positive framing of a concrete institutional change resulting from public scrutiny. Public engagement is highlighted as marginalized within the tender process, receiving negligible scoring weight. Anticipation is entirely absent from the account, as the discussion remains firmly anchored in current or retrospective procurement mechanics rather than exploratory futures. The multi-coded segments reflect a clear narrative arc from systemic institutional inertia to hard-won iterative learning.
transcript:
Interview transcript G05 — Procurement manager, city council
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] Walk me through how this was bought.
[Respondent] Open tender, three bidders, evaluated on price at sixty percent and quality at forty. Within the quality forty there was a sustainability and social value section worth eight, and inside that there was a subsection about stakeholder engagement worth about two and a half percent overall. That two and a half percent is the entire weight the process placed on whether anyone would be consulted.
[Interviewer] Could it have been weighted differently?
[Respondent] Yes, and I'd have supported it. The obstacle is that everything in the quality score has to be assessable in a way that survives a challenge. Price is easy to defend. 'This bidder's engagement plan is better' is exactly the kind of judgement a losing bidder takes to review, and a review costs us more than the contract's margin. So we weight what we can defend, not what matters most.
[Interviewer] Is there any mechanism to check what was promised was delivered?
[Respondent] Contract management, in theory. In practice the contract manager checks the deliverables schedule, and the engagement plan wasn't in the deliverables schedule, it was in the quality submission. Those are different documents and only one of them is monitored. That's a real gap and it exists on most of our contracts, not just this one.
[Interviewer] Has anything changed as a result of this project?
[Respondent] One thing. We now copy the top-scoring quality commitments into the deliverables schedule as contract terms. It was a two-line change to a template. I've been trying to get it done for six years and this project is what finally carried it, because a councillor asked about it in public.
[Interviewer] Would you buy this system the same way again?
[Respondent] With the template change, yes. Without it, I'd have said the process was fine and I'd have been wrong, which is worth noting — for six years I'd have told you our process was fine.
